clue.text: Edna's out in the mountains

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of the name have been knocked out of their usual order

explanation.surface: Someone notes that Edna is away on holiday in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' is the anagram signal: the five letters of EDNA'S, the S included, rearrange into the South American range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are the long mountain chain running down western South America.

clue.text: A jolly girl for the Fleet

parts.note: a Jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A cheerful young woman is cast as the fleet, perhaps in a pageant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective describing the girl, but it is the old naval nickname for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a large fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish one of 1588.

clue.text: Glance at the fixtures-not much on

parts.note: to glance at a page is to scan it
sports fixtures are ties, matches between teams

explanation.surface: A sports fan glances at the list of matches, though there is not much on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not much on' reads as a dull sporting schedule, but it defines skimpy underwear, someone wearing it having little on.
explanation.definitionFit: Scanties are brief women's knickers, so the wearer is barely clothed.

clue.text: Good route for a long-distance driver

definitions.text: Good route for a long-distance driver

parts.words: Good route for a long-distance driver
parts.note: reads as advice for a lorry driver on the motorway, but the driver is a golf club hitting a long tee shot, whose best path is the mown strip of a golf hole

explanation.surface: A trucker looks for the best road for a long haul.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf the driver is the club used for the longest shots; the ideal landing place is the closely mown strip between tee and green, a 'fair' or good way.
explanation.definitionFit: On a golf course this is the short-cut grass a tee shot should land on, between the rough on either side.

clue.text: A place with a unique mode of transport?

definitions.text: A place with a unique mode of transport?

parts.words: A place with a unique mode of transport?
parts.note: read literally, a settlement whose whole transport fleet is a single nag; the idiom means a small, dull, backward place

explanation.surface: A town boasts a transport system unlike any other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unique' suggests something special, but here it means only one: a place so small it has just one animal to pull carts.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a tiny, sleepy settlement with few amenities, originally one so poor it kept just a single animal for haulage.

clue.text: Source of sweetness hard to come by on manoeuvres

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: on manoeuvres, troops are moved about, so these words are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A sweet treat is difficult to obtain while the army is on exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on manoeuvres' signals the anagram, but its ON is fodder too: COME BY ON rearranges to ONEYCOMB after H; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bees store their honey in the wax cells of this structure, so it supplies sweetness.

clue.text: Bound to be performed by the ballet-dancer

definitions.text: Bound to be performed by the ballet-dancer

parts.words: Bound to be performed by the ballet-dancer
parts.note: reads as something a dancer is obliged to do, but bound is a noun, a leap, the kind a dancer does with beating legs

explanation.surface: Something the ballet-dancer is certain to perform on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like 'certain to', but 'Bound' is a noun meaning a jump.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a ballet jump in which the dancer crosses and uncrosses the legs rapidly while in the air.

clue.text: Loner made to become a member of society

indicators.note: made suggests the letters are made into a new shape, the anagram signal here

explanation.surface: A solitary person is forced to join a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' signals the anagram of LONER; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up and be registered as a member of a club or course.

clue.text: Novelist making friends in France

explanation.surface: A writer who makes friends while living in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley and Martin Amis are British novelists; the French word for friends is the same spelling.

clue.text: He will always keep a servant

explanation.surface: Someone who will always employ a household servant.
explanation.definitionFit: One who retains or holds on to something; also a long-serving servant kept in a household.

clue.text: European composer from Harlem

indicators.note: from suggests the composer is made out of these letters, so they are reworked

explanation.surface: A European composer is said to come from the New York neighbourhood of Harlem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is an old-style anagram signal: HARLEM is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Mahler was an Austrian composer of symphonies, born in Bohemia.

clue.text: In Italy male singer lacks tone

indicators.note: lacks means the singer is without the following word, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a baritone is a male singer with a middling voice

explanation.surface: An Italian man's singing voice has no tone to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: 'In Italy' stands for a place in Italy, the southern port city on the Adriatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Bari is a port city in the Puglia region of southern Italy.

clue.text: Not easy to grasp by sailors on land

parts.note: AB is an able seaman, so ABS are sailors
a tract is an area of land

explanation.surface: Sailors ashore find something hard to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' and 'on' are links placing the sailors before the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstract ideas are theoretical rather than concrete, so hard to understand.

clue.text: Frequent praise not unusual

indicators.note: unusual tells the solver these letters appear in an unusual arrangement

explanation.surface: Praise that is commonplace rather than rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frequent' looks like an adjective but is the verb: to frequent a shop. 'unusual' rearranges PRAISE NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To patronise a shop is to be a regular customer there, visiting it often.

clue.text: Mother strangely sweet on famous Hollywood film-star

parts.note: MA is a familiar word for mother

indicators.note: strangely says the following word turns up in an odd order

explanation.surface: Mum is oddly keen on a famous film star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' rearranges SWEET into EWEST; 'on' is a link putting MA first.
explanation.definitionFit: Mae West was a famous American actress of 1930s cinema, known for her innuendo.

clue.text: Betting, using a pay-phone

parts.note: a wage is pay
to ring someone is to phone them

explanation.surface: Someone places bets from a public telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pay-phone' reads as a coin-box telephone, but split in two its halves are separate pieces; 'using a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagering is placing money on an uncertain outcome, the same as gambling.

clue.text: Perplexing situation for retired cover girl

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word for cover is read backwards

parts.note: a lid is a cover
Emma is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A model who once posed for magazine covers has stopped working, leaving her in a quandary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired cover girl' reads as a former magazine model, but 'retired' turns only the cover backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a quandary in which every available choice looks bad.

clue.text: Your ills may turn out to be imaginary

indicators.note: turn out suggests the letters turn round into another arrangement

explanation.surface: A reassuring doctor suggests your ailments are all in the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may turn out' rearranges YOUR ILLS; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illusory is based on illusion, so not real.

clue.text: Visible location for a pub, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the words are spoken and sound like the entry

parts.note: a pub is an inn, and its location its site

explanation.surface: A pub-goer remarks that the tavern stands in a conspicuous spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Split, the entry reads IN SIGHT, which means visible; spoken, it sounds like INN SITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Split as two words the entry means able to be seen, within view.

clue.text: Cow appears in good condition in the marsh

indicators.note: appears in places one word within the other

parts.note: a fen is a marsh, as in East Anglia's Fens
to be in good condition is to be all right, in right order

explanation.surface: A cow looks healthy out in the marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' looks like the animal, but it is the verb meaning to intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to intimidate them, to scare them into submission.

clue.text: See 5
Foreign dance circle lost member

indicators.note: lost means the circle has gone missing from the dance

parts.note: the limbo is a West Indian dance under a lowered bar
O is round like a circle

explanation.surface: A dancer from abroad lost a leg in the circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' is not a club member but an arm or leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb is a member of the body, an arm or a leg.

clue.text: Threaten to give me the R cane, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster warns a pupil he will be caned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges CANE into NACE after ME; 'to give', 'the' and the stray R (likely a scanning mark) are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To menace someone is to threaten or intimidate them.

clue.text: What might be there in the atmosphere

indicators.note: might be says the following letters could become a different word

parts.note: the letters also run forwards across 'be there', a coincidence: the setter's device is the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A question about what is present in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges THERE; 'What' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether is the upper air or clear sky, in old poetic use.

clue.text: He provides a new setting for the doctor

indicators.note: a setting holds a jewel, so these words hold the doctor inside them

parts.note: taken as written
DR is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A man arranges a fresh location for his GP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' is the definition: any man's name will do. DR goes inside A NEW.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew is a common man's name.

clue.text: The point in folly that becomes madness

indicators.note: in places the point inside the folly

parts.note: inanity is foolish silliness
S is south, a compass point

explanation.surface: Folly taken to its logical end becomes madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' is a compass point, S, not the purpose of something; 'that becomes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Insanity is serious mental illness, derangement.

clue.text: Spending some surplus in gold

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone is spending part of their reserve of gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts inside surplUS and finishes in gold-less IN G of 'in gold'.
explanation.definitionFit: Using up money or supplies is consuming them, as in expenditure.

clue.text: Letter or card

explanation.surface: A note or postcard.
explanation.definitionFit: A written symbol such as a letter of the alphabet; and an eccentric, amusing person, called a card.
